name: Late blight
summary: One of the most destructive tomato diseases. In cool, wet weather it can kill a field in under two weeks.
symptoms: Large, irregular grey-green patches on leaves that quickly turn dark brown
White, fuzzy growth on the underside of leaves in humid mornings
Dark, greasy-looking streaks on stems
Firm brown blotches on green fruit that spread across the fruit
conditions: Cool nights (10–20°C), long periods of leaf wetness, fog and rain. Common in Ghana's highland areas and during the main rainy season.
spread: Spores blow between fields on wind and rain splash, and travel on infected seedlings and potato tubers.
cultural: Remove and burn or bury infected plants immediately
Stake and prune plants so leaves dry quickly
Water at the base in the morning, never in the evening
Do not plant tomato next to potato
organic: Copper-based sprays (copper hydroxide or copper oxychloride) applied before rain and repeated every 5–7 days in wet weather.
chemical: Protectant fungicides containing mancozeb, or systemic products combining metalaxyl and mancozeb. Rotate active ingredients to avoid resistance.
prevention: Destroy volunteer tomato and potato plants after harvest

name: Early blight
summary: A common leaf disease that starts on older, lower leaves and works its way up, reducing yield and exposing fruit to sunscald.
symptoms: Brown spots with rings inside them, like a target or bullseye
Yellowing of the leaf around each spot
Spots appear first on the oldest, lowest leaves
Dark, sunken spots near the stem end of fruit
conditions: Warm temperatures (24–29°C) with alternating wet and dry periods. Worse on stressed or poorly fed plants.
spread: Spores survive in crop debris and soil, and splash onto lower leaves during rain or overhead watering.
cultural: Remove the lowest leaves once plants are established
Mulch to stop soil splashing onto leaves
Feed plants well — balanced fertiliser reduces damage
Rotate away from tomato, pepper, potato and garden egg for 2–3 seasons
organic: Neem-based sprays or copper fungicides every 7–10 days once spots appear.
chemical: Fungicides containing mancozeb, chlorothalonil or azoxystrobin, following label intervals.
prevention: Clear and burn crop debris after harvest
Start with clean seed and seedlings

name: Bacterial spot
summary: A bacterial disease that thrives in hot, rainy weather and spots leaves and fruit, lowering market value.
symptoms: Small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves, often with a yellow halo
Spots merge and leaves turn yellow and drop
Raised, scabby spots on fruit
Defoliation that exposes fruit to sunscald
conditions: Warm (24–30°C), wet and windy weather. Driving rain spreads it fastest.
spread: Carried on seed and transplants; splashes between plants in rain, irrigation, and on hands and tools.
cultural: Avoid working among plants when they are wet
Disinfect stakes and tools between seasons
Use drip or furrow irrigation instead of overhead watering
organic: Copper sprays slow the spread on new growth; begin at the first sign of spots.
chemical: Copper hydroxide, sometimes combined with mancozeb to improve control. Antibiotics are not recommended.
prevention: Use certified seed or hot-water-treated seed
Rotate for at least two seasons
Control weeds from the tomato family

name: Leaf mold
summary: A humid-weather disease, especially in greenhouses and dense plantings, that causes leaves to yellow and wither.
symptoms: Pale green or yellow patches on the upper leaf surface
Olive-green to brown velvety mould on the underside, directly beneath
Leaves curl, wither and drop
Rarely affects fruit
conditions: Very high humidity (above 85%) with mild to warm temperatures and poor ventilation.
spread: Spores move on air currents and on workers' clothing; the fungus survives on plant debris.
cultural: Improve airflow by pruning and wider spacing
organic: Copper or sulphur-based sprays, with good coverage of the leaf underside.
chemical: Fungicides containing chlorothalonil or mancozeb; follow the label.

name: Septoria leaf spot
summary: Produces many small spots on lower leaves; heavy infections strip plants of foliage during fruiting.
symptoms: Many small, round spots with dark borders and grey or tan centres
Tiny black dots inside the spots
Lower leaves yellow and drop first
Fruit is rarely affected directly
conditions: Warm, wet weather with frequent rain or overhead irrigation.
spread: Spores splash from infected debris and weeds onto lower leaves.
organic: Copper fungicide sprays every 7–10 days in wet periods.
chemical: Chlorothalonil or mancozeb-based fungicides.
prevention: Control nightshade weeds that host the fungus

name: Spider mites
summary: Tiny sap-sucking pests that multiply quickly in hot, dry weather and can bleach and kill leaves.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white speckling on leaves
Leaves turn bronze, dry out and drop
Fine webbing on the underside of leaves and between stems
Tiny moving dots visible under a hand lens
conditions: Hot, dry, dusty conditions — typical of the dry season and Harmattan.
spread: Mites crawl between touching plants and are carried by wind, clothing and tools.
cultural: Spray the underside of leaves with a strong jet of water
Keep plants well watered to reduce stress
organic: Neem oil or insecticidal soap sprayed on the underside of leaves every 5–7 days.
chemical: A registered miticide such as abamectin. Rotate products — mites develop resistance fast.
prevention: Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill predatory mites
Inspect leaf undersides weekly in dry weather

name: Target spot
summary: A warm, humid-weather disease that spots leaves, stems and fruit and is common in the tropics.
symptoms: Brown spots with light centres and faint rings
Spots may crack in the middle
Sunken spots on fruit
Leaf drop starting from the lower canopy
conditions: Warm temperatures and high humidity or long periods of leaf wetness.
spread: Survives on crop debris and many weed hosts; spores travel on wind and splash.
cultural: Prune for airflow and stake plants
organic: Copper-based sprays at the first sign of spots.
chemical: Fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb or azoxystrobin; rotate modes of action.
prevention: Rotate with non-host crops such as maize
Clear weeds and debris after harvest

name: Yellow leaf curl virus
summary: Spread by whiteflies. Plants infected young may produce almost no fruit. There is no cure once a plant is infected.
symptoms: Small, upward-curling leaves with yellow edges
Stunted plants with a bushy top
Flowers drop and few fruit set
Whiteflies on the underside of leaves
conditions: Warm, dry periods when whitefly numbers are high.
spread: Carried from plant to plant by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci. Not spread by seed.
cultural: Uproot and destroy infected plants early
Use yellow sticky traps to monitor and reduce whiteflies
organic: Neem-based sprays and reflective mulches reduce whitefly feeding.
chemical: There is no chemical cure for the virus. An extension officer can advise a registered insecticide for whitefly control.
prevention: Avoid planting next to older, infected tomato fields
Leave a tomato-free break between seasons

name: Mosaic virus
summary: A very stable virus spread by hands and tools. It reduces vigour and fruit quality and has no cure.
symptoms: Light and dark green mottled pattern on leaves
Distorted, fern-like or narrow leaves
Stunted growth
Uneven ripening or brown streaks inside fruit
conditions: Any conditions — spreads wherever plants are handled.
spread: By touch: hands, tools, clothing and pruning. Survives for months in debris and on seed.
cultural: Wash hands with soap before handling plants
Disinfect tools in a bleach or milk solution
Do not smoke or handle tobacco near tomato plants
organic: No treatment cures the virus; focus on hygiene and removal.
chemical: No chemical cure exists. Prevention is the only control.
prevention: Rotate away from tomato and pepper

name: Late blight
summary: The disease behind the Irish potato famine. It destroys leaves and rots tubers in storage.
symptoms: Dark, water-soaked patches on leaf tips and edges
White mould on the underside of leaves in humid weather
Blackened stems and collapsing plants
Reddish-brown rot just under the tuber skin
conditions: Cool, wet, humid weather — especially in highland growing areas.
spread: Wind-blown spores, rain splash and infected seed tubers.
cultural: Hill soil up around plants to protect tubers
organic: Copper-based sprays applied preventively in wet weather.
chemical: Mancozeb protectants or metalaxyl-plus-mancozeb systemic fungicides, rotated.
prevention: Harvest in dry weather and store only sound tubers

name: Early blight
summary: Causes target-like spots on older leaves and can reduce tuber size when leaves die early.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on older leaves
Yellowing around the spots
Leaves die from the bottom of the plant upwards
Dark, sunken lesions on tubers
conditions: Warm days, dew or rain, and plants under stress from drought or low fertility.
spread: Survives in soil and debris; spores splash onto leaves.
organic: Copper or neem sprays at first symptoms.
chemical: Mancozeb, chlorothalonil or azoxystrobin-based fungicides.
prevention: Avoid water stress during tuber formation

name: Gray leaf spot
summary: A major maize leaf disease in humid areas. Severe infections before grain fill cut yields sharply.
symptoms: Long, narrow, rectangular grey or tan lesions running between leaf veins
Lesions merge and leaves die
Starts on lower leaves and moves up
Weakened stalks prone to lodging
conditions: Warm temperatures with high humidity, heavy dew and fog.
spread: The fungus survives on maize residue left on the surface and spreads by wind and splash.
cultural: Rotate maize with legumes such as cowpea or soybean
organic: No reliable organic spray; rely on rotation, residue management and resistant varieties.
chemical: Strobilurin or triazole fungicides at early tasselling when disease pressure is high.
prevention: Plant tolerant varieties recommended for your zone
Plant early in the season to avoid peak humidity at grain fill

name: Common rust
summary: Produces rusty pustules on leaves. Usually a minor problem, but heavy early infections reduce yield.
symptoms: Small, raised, cinnamon-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces
Pustules release rust-coloured powder when rubbed
Pustules turn dark brown to black later in the season
Yellowing of heavily infected leaves
conditions: Cool to moderate temperatures (16–25°C) with high humidity and dew.
spread: Spores blow long distances on the wind.
cultural: Plant early to avoid peak spore periods
organic: Sulphur-based sprays can help on small plots.
chemical: Triazole or strobilurin fungicides, only if severe infection appears before tasselling.
prevention: Monitor leaves from knee height onwards

name: Northern leaf blight
summary: Causes long cigar-shaped lesions. Infection before silking can cause significant yield loss.
symptoms: Long (2.5–15 cm), cigar-shaped, grey-green to tan lesions
Lesions start on lower leaves
Dark spore growth on lesions in humid weather
Large areas of dead leaf tissue
conditions: Moderate temperatures (18–27°C) with heavy dew and long wet periods.
spread: Survives on maize residue; spores spread by wind and rain.
cultural: Manage residue by burying or removing it
organic: No dependable organic spray; prioritise resistant varieties and rotation.
chemical: Fungicides such as azoxystrobin or propiconazole if lesions appear on upper leaves before silking.
prevention: Scout fields regularly from the knee-high stage

name: Bacterial spot
summary: The most important bacterial disease of pepper in warm, wet regions; causes leaf drop and spotted fruit.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown
Yellowing leaves that drop early
Raised, scabby spots on fruit
Sunscald on fruit exposed by leaf loss
conditions: Warm, wet, windy weather and overhead irrigation.
spread: Seed, transplants, rain splash, and handling wet plants.
cultural: Rotate away from pepper and tomato
organic: Copper sprays started early and repeated during wet periods.
chemical: Copper hydroxide with mancozeb improves control. Antibiotics are not advised.

name: Citrus greening (HLB)
summary: A deadly, incurable citrus disease spread by psyllid insects. Infected trees decline and die within years.
symptoms: Blotchy, uneven yellowing of leaves (not symmetrical)
Small, lopsided fruit that stays green at the bottom
Bitter fruit with aborted seeds
Twig dieback and heavy fruit drop
conditions: Anywhere the psyllid insect vector is present.
spread: Spread by citrus psyllids feeding on new shoots, and by grafting infected budwood.
cultural: Remove and destroy infected trees to protect the orchard
Control psyllids on new flush growth
Report suspected cases to an extension officer
organic: Neem and horticultural oils reduce psyllid numbers but do not cure infected trees.
chemical: No cure exists. Registered insecticides for psyllid control, as advised by an officer.
prevention: Buy seedlings only from certified nurseries
Inspect new growth regularly for psyllids

name: Bacterial spot
summary: Spots and holes in leaves, and pitted, cracked fruit in warm, wet weather.
symptoms: Small angular spots on leaves that fall out, leaving shot-holes
Yellowing and early leaf drop
Pitted, cracked spots on fruit
Cankers on twigs
conditions: Warm, wet, windy weather.
spread: Rain splash and wind from twig cankers.
organic: Copper sprays during dormancy and early season.
chemical: Copper-based bactericides; follow the label for timing.

name: Apple scab
summary: Olive-green to black scabby spots on leaves and fruit that reduce fruit quality.
symptoms: Olive-green velvety spots on leaves
Dark, corky scabs on fruit
Early leaf drop
conditions: Cool, wet spring-like weather.
spread: Spores from fallen infected leaves.
cultural: Rake up and destroy fallen leaves
organic: Sulphur or copper sprays during wet periods.
chemical: Protectant fungicides such as captan or mancozeb.

name: Black rot
summary: Causes leaf spots, fruit rot and branch cankers.
symptoms: Purple-edged 'frog-eye' leaf spots
Rotting fruit with rings
Sunken cankers on branches
conditions: Warm, humid weather.
spread: Spores from mummified fruit and cankers.
cultural: Remove mummified fruit and dead wood
organic: Copper sprays in wet periods.
chemical: Captan or other registered fungicides.
prevention: Keep trees vigorous and well pruned

name: Cedar apple rust
summary: Bright orange spots on leaves; needs juniper trees nearby to complete its life cycle.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on leaves
Small cups or tubes under the spots
Early leaf drop in severe cases
conditions: Wet spring weather near juniper or cedar trees.
spread: Spores travel between apple and juniper hosts.
cultural: Remove nearby juniper hosts where practical
organic: Sulphur sprays at early leaf stage.
chemical: Registered rust fungicides such as myclobutanil.

name: Powdery mildew
summary: A white powdery coating on young leaves and shoots.
symptoms: White powdery patches on leaves
Curled, distorted young leaves
conditions: Warm days with humid nights; does not need rain.
spread: Wind-blown spores.
organic: Sulphur or potassium bicarbonate sprays.
chemical: Registered mildew fungicides.

name: Black rot
summary: Can destroy a whole crop by turning berries into hard, black mummies.
symptoms: Tan leaf spots with dark borders
Berries shrivel into hard black mummies
conditions: Warm, wet weather.
spread: Spores from mummified berries.
cultural: Remove all mummies and infected canes
organic: Copper sprays from early shoot growth.
chemical: Mancozeb or myclobutanil fungicides.
prevention: Keep vineyards clean over the off-season

name: Esca (black measles)
summary: A trunk disease that causes striped leaves and spotted berries, and can kill vines.
symptoms: 'Tiger-stripe' yellow and brown leaf patterns
Dark spots on berries
Sudden wilting of vines
conditions: Enters through pruning wounds; worse under drought stress.
spread: Spores infect fresh pruning cuts.
organic: Seal large pruning wounds.
chemical: No effective cure; wound protectants reduce infection.

name: Leaf blight
summary: Dark irregular spots that cause early leaf drop late in the season.
symptoms: Dark brown, irregular spots on leaves
Yellowing and early leaf fall
conditions: Warm, humid conditions.
spread: Spores from infected leaves.
organic: Copper sprays.
chemical: Mancozeb-based fungicides.

name: Powdery mildew
summary: A white powder on leaves that weakens plants and reduces fruit size and storage life.
symptoms: White powdery spots on upper leaves
Spots spread to cover leaves
Leaves yellow, dry and die
conditions: Warm days, cool nights and shade; spreads even in dry weather.
spread: Wind-blown spores.
cultural: Space plants and plant in full sun
organic: Sulphur, potassium bicarbonate or diluted milk sprays weekly.
chemical: Registered fungicides for cucurbit mildew; rotate products.

name: Leaf scorch
summary: Purple spots that merge until leaves look burnt.
symptoms: Small dark purple spots on leaves
Leaves turn brown and look scorched
conditions: Warm, wet weather.
spread: Spores splash from infected leaves.
organic: Copper sprays.
chemical: Captan or other registered fungicides.
